text: [da-2024-review] The DA says Cornell police asked his office in November 2024 to review the former student's six-page signed statement, that several prosecutors and investigators reviewed it assuming its facts were true, and that they concluded those facts did not meet the elements of a crime under New York law. He says her credibility was never in question.

[da-describes-statement] The DA describes the November 2024 sworn statement as not alleging drugging against her will or a gang rape, and as describing her drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious and consensual. This is the DA's characterization; the statement has not been released in full and her attorney disputes it.

[penal-law-mental-incapacity] Under New York Penal Law 130.00(6), a person counts as 'mentally incapacitated' (and so unable to consent) only when the intoxicating substance was given to them without their consent, or another act was done to them without their consent. Intoxication the person chose does not meet this definition.

[da-legal-analysis] Applying Penal Law 130.05, the DA wrote that her statement did not describe physical force, a drug given without consent, unconsciousness, or a clear refusal that was ignored, and that by the statement's account the sexual conduct stopped each time she asked. This reading of the statement is disputed.

[governor-names-law-gap] Gov. Hochul, while criticizing Cornell police and the DA, also said the case exposed 'a gap in State law': in her words, if someone is too intoxicated to consent, it should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol. She said she will work with the Legislature to change it.

[da-law-barred-incapacity-only] After his removal, the DA said he supports the attorney general's appointment but still holds that New York law did not let him prosecute based only on her account that she was too incapacitated to consent. AP notes that under state law, being too drunk or high to consent is not necessarily enough for a rape charge.

[da-offered-meeting] The DA says that, under his standing policy, his office asked Cornell police to tell the former student she could meet with prosecutors to have the decision explained and ask questions, and that Cornell police then explained the result to her. This is the DA's account; no response from her side on this point was found.

[da-not-contacted] The DA says neither the former student nor her attorneys contacted his office in the nearly two years after the 2024 decision, either to say the statement was inaccurate or to ask for reconsideration, and that he reached out to her attorneys after the lawsuit was filed.

[cornell-nov-2024-interim-steps] Cornell put the Chi Phi Xi chapter under a temporary suspension order on Nov. 8, 2024, and in late November 2024 issued interim temporary suspensions to a number of students while campus police and the Title IX office investigated.

[cupd-further-investigation] Documents reviewed by ABC News show that by Nov. 25, 2024, Cornell police had followed up anonymous tips, interviewed witnesses, contacted the accused men's lawyers, and issued 'persona non grata' notices barring several fraternity members from parts of campus.

[da-nothing-to-review] Asked about the further interviews Cornell police flagged in November 2024, the DA said the fraternity members had declined to be interviewed on their lawyers' advice, so 'there was nothing to review.' NBC News reports that police files did contain witness interviews and tips, so this point is disputed.

[snapchat-screenshot-sent] Cornell says its police gave the DA the Snapchat group-chat screenshots in November 2024. The DA told CNN the screenshots were not part of his office's initial analysis but that Cornell had them and sent them to his team. He described them as having nothing to do with her consent.

[statement-read-back-and-signed] According to the interview transcript reported by CBS News New York, the Cornell police investigator read her account back and asked her to correct it. On the second day she reviewed the revised six-page statement, after her adviser asked whether she wanted two advisers to review it, and said she was 'very confident' about it before signing.

[cupd-jurisdiction] Cornell says its police officers are special deputy sheriffs under New York Education Law 5709, with law-enforcement duties on Cornell property, and that the incident happened in Cornell's jurisdiction.

[title-ix-scope-timeline] According to court records reported by CNY Central, Cornell's Title IX investigator did more than 50 interviews between December 2024 and March 2025 and issued an investigative report on April 16, 2025. A three-member panel then held 12 days of hearings in May 2025.

[cornell-sanctions-statement] Cornell says its Title IX hearing panel issued sanctions that included expulsions and suspensions, and that no accused student was offered essays as a sole consequence. The lawsuit alleges the accused could reduce their sanctions by writing essays, so this point is disputed.

[sanctions-breakdown-nyt] Discipline summaries obtained by The New York Times show that two of the seven men were expelled, one who had already graduated was barred from campus, two were suspended, and two received lighter sanctions (reflection papers and training). The summaries also show the panel did not conclude she was sexually assaulted by all the men she accused.

[court-upheld-title-ix-procedure] A Tompkins County Supreme Court judge dismissed one accused man's challenge to Cornell's Title IX process. The judge found Cornell gave adequate notice and substantially followed its procedures. In that case the panel found the man not responsible for sexual assault but responsible for attempted sexual exploitation. He has appealed.

[cornell-privacy-position] Cornell says federal privacy law prevents it from disclosing information about individual students, so it will not publicly confirm each person's sanction. It says it will respond in detail through the legal process. FERPA's own exceptions make the extent of this limit contested.

[ferpa-final-results-exception] Federal FERPA regulations list an exception allowing a college to disclose, without consent, the final results of a disciplinary proceeding if it finds the student is an alleged perpetrator of a crime of violence or non-forcible sex offense who violated school rules. This qualifies Cornell's statement that privacy law bars disclosure.

[da-declined-further-material] Documents reviewed by ABC News (first reported by The New York Times) show the DA's office did not review material gathered by Cornell police beyond the six-page summary of her statements before deciding against charges. A Nov. 25, 2024 call note records the DA's office saying charges would not be pursued.

[first-record-8-10-men] Per documents obtained by ABC News, Cornell police's first record says she reported being raped by 8-10 men at the fraternity house. That language did not appear in the condensed statement Cornell police prepared and sent to the DA.

[transcript-100-percent] CBS News New York reports that the transcript of her November 2024 interview with Cornell police shows she said she could say with 100% confidence she was raped. The DA says he never saw the transcript and relied on the signed statement.

[attorney-disputes-difference] The former student's attorney told CNN that the Cornell police report prepared after she gave her statement is 'not materially different' from the lawsuit's account. He said the complaint is longer because he met with her several times.

[governor-faults-handoff] Gov. Hochul said the words in which the former student said she was raped never reached prosecutors in Cornell police's account. She also said the DA declined charges after reviewing that incomplete account without interviewing her. She cited this when she made the attorney general special prosecutor.

[alleged] The civil complaint alleges the former student was drugged and raped by multiple members of the Chi Phi Xi chapter at the fraternity house on Cornell's campus. These are allegations in an unresolved civil case; no one has been criminally charged.

[alleged] The complaint alleges Cornell knew or should have known the chapter had a history of ketamine use, and, 'upon information and belief,' that police responded to a drug-related incident at the house one week before the alleged assault.

[reported] ABC News reports that a report from Cornell's own Title IX process found ketamine was used by multiple people at the house at the time, including a redacted person who overdosed on or about Oct. 18, 2024. Among sources opened for this research, this is the only support outside the complaint for drug use at the house; it does not show what Cornell knew before Oct. 19.

[alleged] The complaint alleges that the seven accused members, who received temporary suspensions around Nov. 8, 2024, were allowed to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell. Cornell disputes this.

[reported] On Nov. 8, 2024, a Cornell crime alert reported that an individual said she was sexually assaulted by several males and coerced into consuming ketamine and other drugs at a fraternity on Edgemoor Lane. The alert gave the date as Oct. 25, which differs from the Oct. 19-20 date in later records.

[established] Cornell's interim president wrote on Nov. 26, 2024 that the chapter had been under a temporary suspension order since Nov. 8, 2024, and that interim temporary suspensions had been issued to a number of students the previous week, while Cornell police continued a criminal investigation.

[reported] According to court records reported by CNY Central (a letter from Cornell's counsel), the Title IX hearing panel held 12 days of hearings in May 2025, deliberated in June-July 2025, and issued its decision on all seven accused on Aug. 18, 2025.

[established] The DA says the statement Cornell police brought to his office was a six-page, single-spaced, typed statement that the former student signed and annotated with more than 20 handwritten notes.

[established] The DA says multiple prosecutors and criminal investigators reviewed the statement in November 2024, assumed it true, and concluded that the facts as written did not meet the elements of a crime under New York law.

[disputed] The DA describes her November 2024 sworn statement as not alleging she was drugged against her will or gang raped, and as describing her drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual. Her attorney and the governor dispute that this reflects what she told police.

[reported] Documents reviewed by ABC News (first reported by The New York Times) show that on Nov. 25, 2024, a Cornell police investigator told a DA investigator about further interviews, and the DA's office did not review material beyond the six-page summary.

[reported] According to an interview transcript obtained by CBS New York and reported by AP, she told Cornell police weeks after the incident that she could say with 100% confidence she was raped. The transcript has not been publicly released.

[reported] The DA told CBS News New York that the '100% confidence' statement was not information his office had, called it a legal conclusion, and said that if she had said those words his office would have wanted to explore that more.

[reported] The DA told CNN the only materials prosecutors received in 2024 were the six-page statement and Snapchat messages exchanged by fraternity members during the incident; he said Cornell's Title IX material was never seen by his office.

[established] Cornell's FAQ (as of Oct. 8, 2026) says Cornell police shared her sworn statement and the Snapchat screenshot with the DA's office, which it calls established protocol when police believe a crime may have occurred, and says the 2024 charging decision was the DA's, not Cornell's.
[reported] An earlier version of Cornell's FAQ said its police shared 'all investigatory information' with the DA's office; WSKG/NPR found that line had been removed by Sept. 30, 2026.

[established] Cornell says its police department is a unit of the university whose officers are special deputy sheriffs under New York Education Law 5709, and that the incident occurred in Cornell's jurisdiction.
[reported] The Ithaca Police Department said the incident was never reported to it and that it learned of the allegations through the media in September 2026.

[disputed] Cornell says its Title IX hearing panel issued sanctions that included expulsions and suspensions, and that none of the accused was offered essays as a sole consequence. Cornell gives no numbers, citing federal privacy law; the lawsuit's essay allegation conflicts with this account.

[reported] Per a court ruling reported by CNY Central, one accused member was found responsible only for attempted sexual exploitation (not sexual assault), and his sanctions included a one-way no-contact order, a class, and a reflection paper. A judge upheld Cornell's process for him; he has appealed.

[reported] CBS News reports that, according to the school, two of the seven men were expelled, two were suspended for at least two semesters, one had graduated before any punishment, and two were found not responsible for sexual misconduct. Cornell's public statements give no such numbers.

[established] Cornell formed the Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault in spring 2025 and released its final recommendations on March 17, 2026, including a public health campaign and clearer information on reporting options.
[established] On Sept. 29, 2026, Gov. Hochul said she supported the DA reopening the case and called for outside counsel to conduct an independent review of Cornell's response.

[established] On Oct. 6, 2026, a special committee of Cornell's trustees hired a former U.S. deputy attorney general at King & Spalding to lead an independent review covering how reports are investigated, campus police, and coordination with prosecutors, including Cornell's handling of this case.

[established] Under New York Education Law 5703, the governor is an ex officio member of Cornell's board of trustees during her term. This bears on questions about the independence of reviews the governor has called for or ordered.
